sections.normalized_html:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the function [MATH: y=\tan x?] Assume that [MATH: n] is an integer.

  1. The zeros of the function are at [MATH: x = \pi n.]

  2. The function has asymptotes at [MATH: x = 2\pi n.]

  3. The range of the function is [MATH: y\in [-1,1].]
sections.readable_text:
Which of the following statements are true regarding the function [MATH: y=\tan x?] Assume that [MATH: n] is an integer.

1. The zeros of the function are at [MATH: x = \pi n.]
2. The function has asymptotes at [MATH: x = 2\pi n.]
3. The range of the function is [MATH: y\in [-1,1].]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Let's plot the graph of [MATH: y=\tan x.]

Let's go through each statement.

  • Statement I is true. The zeros occur at [MATH: x=0, \pm \pi, \pm2\pi,\ldots,] which can be written as [MATH: x=n\pi.]

  • Statement II is false. The function has an asymptote at [MATH: x = \dfrac \pi 2] and the period is [MATH: \pi.] Therefore, the asymptotes occur at [MATH: x = \dfrac \pi 2 + \pi n.]

  • Statement III is false. The function takes values on all the real numbers, hence the range is [MATH: y\in (-\infty, \infty).]

So, the correct answer is "I only".

sections.normalized_html: If [MATH: \tan\left( x\right) = -2] for some value of [MATH: x,] then find the value of [MATH: \tan\left( x-2\pi\right).]
sections.readable_text: If [MATH: \tan\left( x\right) = -2] for some value of [MATH: x,] then find the value of [MATH: \tan\left( x-2\pi\right).]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
The period of [MATH: y=\tan x] is [MATH: \pi.] Therefore, for any integer [MATH: n,] we have [MATH: \tan x = \tan (x+n\pi).]

Substituting [MATH: n=-2] into the above gives

[MATH: \tan x|= \tan (x + (− 2) ⋅ π) = \tan (x − 2π).]

Since [MATH: \tan\left( x\right) = -2,] we get that [MATH: \tan\left( x-2\pi\right) = -2.]

Recall that a function [MATH: f(x)] is odd if it satisfies the property

Content:
As it turns out, tangent is an odd function! So, for any value of [MATH: x,] we have

Odd functions always have rotational symmetry of order [MATH: 2] about the origin. This is indeed true of the tangent function, as we can see from the diagram below.

items.title: Utilizing the Oddness Property of the Tangent Function

sections.normalized_html: If [MATH: \tan x = -\dfrac{2}{3},] find the value of [MATH: \tan (-x+7\pi).]
sections.readable_text: If [MATH: \tan x = -\dfrac{2}{3},] find the value of [MATH: \tan (-x+7\pi).]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, let's recall the graph of [MATH: y=\tan{x}.]

From the graph, we note the following:

  • The period of [MATH: \tan{x}] is [MATH: \pi.]

  • Our graph has rotational symmetry of order [MATH: 2] about the origin. This means that [MATH: \tan{x}] is an odd function, and we have [MATH: \tan(-x) = -\tan{x}.]

Let's now evaluate our expression:

  • Firstly, using the periodicity of [MATH: \tan{x},] we have [MATH: \tan (− x + 7π)|= \tan (− x + π ⋅ 7); = \tan (− x).]

  • Secondly, using the oddness of [MATH: \tan{x},] we have [MATH: \tan (− x)|= − \tan x; = − (− (2)/(3)).]

Therefore, [MATH: \tan (-x+7\pi)=\dfrac{2}{3}.]

Item 10 — Example: Utilizing the Oddness Property of the Tangent Function

Example Prompt:
If [MATH: \tan x = -\dfrac{2}{3},] find the value of [MATH: \tan (-x+7\pi).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, let's recall the graph of [MATH: y=\tan{x}.]

[IMG: /graphics/d01abb298d92d64b71126490ab06b4ed]

From the graph, we note the following:

- The period of [MATH: \tan{x}] is [MATH: \pi.]
- Our graph has rotational symmetry of order [MATH: 2] about the origin. This means that [MATH: \tan{x}] is an odd function, and we have
[MATH: \tan(-x) = -\tan{x}.]

Let's now evaluate our expression:

- Firstly, using the periodicity of [MATH: \tan{x},] we have
[MATH: \tan (− x + 7π)|= \tan (− x + π ⋅ 7); = \tan (− x).]
- Secondly, using the oddness of [MATH: \tan{x},] we have
[MATH: \tan (− x)|= − \tan x; = − (− (2)/(3)).]

Therefore, [MATH: \tan (-x+7\pi)=\dfrac{2}{3}.]
